title: Decasia (2002) and They Shall Not Grow Old (2018) - Radically different approaches to the decay of time

commenti.body:
>It's highly reminiscent of The Caretaker's music project *Everywhere at the End of Time* (2016-2019), which in turn took the Caretaker name and a large chunk of inspiration from Stanley Kubrick's *The Shining* (1980). In that multi-album piece, old big-band dance records were put through various layers of sound distortion and degradation to approximate the experience of Alzheimer's and dementia.

It's certainly the other way around, no? That the aesthetic of The Caretaker project is reminiscent of this film? As you yourself write, one predates the other by fourteen years.

I appreciate you spotlighting these two films, both of which I truly enjoyed. 

I do have a slightly different interpretation of *Decasia*. Yes, it's absolutely about death and decay and the ravages -- that's there in the title. But it's also, more than any film I can ever think of, about the physical medium of film itself, both its fragility and its amazing ability to survive and to preserve the past. 

Have you ever seen *Dawson City: Frozen Time*? It's a sort of spiritual sequel to *Decasia* and, in a very real sense, a film about life and survival and endurance to *Decasia*'s death and decay.

I think my wording in that bit is not as clear as it could be. I shouldn't have said 'reminiscent' which implies one influences the other. I have no evidence that the film influences the Caretaker project and obviously it couldn't be the other way round. 

I only meant in this case that the approach of the film reminded me of the music project, as that's the way I encountered them. 

Thanks for the recommendation of Dawson City, never heard of it before and will certainly look into it.

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oEbHM8Vsvlo&t=42s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oEbHM8Vsvlo&t=42s)

Bill Morrison is in my opinion one of the most original, creative and underappreciated filmmakers working today.
Can you think of a fiction film that really does a good job at representing the passing of time?

Damned good question. There are those that do a good job at showing the effects of time like The Father, which is brought to mind by the mention of the Caretaker music. 

Will consider and come back on that soon.
